The base paper is:
Title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD

A previous critical-appraisal step produced the following 15 limitations of the base paper:

G1. Limited explicit limitation and future-work reporting: MVFA-AD lacks a dedicated limitations section; its only explicit scope caveat is that in-domain evaluation is treated as secondary, and its future-work statements are generic. The remaining limitations discussed here were therefore inferred from the protocol, architecture, and evaluation design rather than drawn from authorial disclosure.
G2. The zero-shot protocol is not modality- or anatomy-disjoint: The BMAD leave-one-out setting includes two retinal OCT datasets, RESC and OCT17; when one is held out, the other remains in the training set. For these pairs, evaluation does not test an unseen medical modality or anatomy, which may inflate the reported OCT results. A valid zero-shot protocol should instead group and hold out by modality, anatomy, acquisition device, and site simultaneously.
G3. Annotation requirements remain clinically heavy: The adaptation objective is trained on pixel-level anomaly-segmentation masks using a combination of Dice, Focal, and binary cross-entropy losses across four feature levels, including under zero-shot evaluation. This effectively requires dense expert annotation for every training image; the method does not formulate an image-level-only, sparse, or normal-only supervision variant, which weakens its relevance to label-scarce clinical settings.
G4. The few-shot setting is underspecified and operationally costly: The K annotated target images must simultaneously supply normal exemplars for the memory bank and abnormal examples for adapter training, yet the partition between the two is left unspecified; for K = 2 this may be infeasible if sufficient exemplars of both classes are required. Clinical few-shot supervision, in practice, may contain only normal or entirely unlabeled data. The method further implies per-task retraining, yet training time and computational cost are not reported.
G5. Prompting is static, generic, and domain-agnostic: The text encoder is kept frozen, and the prompts consist of hand-crafted normal/abnormal state descriptions averaged over 35 ImageNet templates. This design presumes a single, universal visual-language concept of “normal” and “abnormal” that holds uniformly across imaging modalities, and it omits instance-adaptive, visually conditioned, or hybrid prompting strategies. No prompt-sensitivity analysis is provided.
G6. Anomaly modeling is binary and lacks clinical granularity: All anomalies are collapsed into a single “abnormal” class. The model performs no differentiation of benign-versus-malignant status, anomaly subcategory, severity, radiological sign, or differential cost, despite clinical workflows requiring category-specific actionability and support for multi-anomaly detection within a single case.
G7. Normal/anomaly disentanglement and distributional asymmetry are not made explicit: The dual- adapter design separates anomaly-classification and anomaly-segmentation features, but it does not explicitly model the compact distribution of normal samples against the comparatively diverse distribution of abnormal samples. The method relies on shared adapted features and a few-shot normal memory bank without routing mechanisms, dual normal/abnormal pathways, or many-to- one, SigLIP-style regularization.
G8. Architecture, fusion, and hyperparameters are under-ablated and partly unclear: Numerous design choices — including γ = 0.1, λ = 1.0, four feature levels, an input resolution of 240, a learning rate of 10−3, a batch size of 16, 50 training epochs, β = 0.5, and fixed prompt templates — are presented without accompanying sensitivity analysis. The adapter and projector equations and their class-token handling are dimensionally unclear, and the partitioning of the 24-layer Vision Transformer into four stages is non-standard, which hinders reproducibility. The final score fusion combines zero-shot softmax probabilities on the interval [0, 1] with few-shot cosine distances on the interval [0, 2] using a fixed weight of 0.5, without normalization or calibration, so that one branch may arbitrarily dominate the fused score.
G9. Classification and aggregation are outlier-sensitive: Image-level anomaly classification is obtained via max-aggregation over pixel-level anomaly scores, so that a single spurious high-scoring pixel is sufficient to produce a false positive. No robust aggregation, calibration, or uncertainty-estimation mechanism is employed to mitigate this sensitivity.
G10. Evaluation lacks patient-level leakage controls and variance estimates: Patient-level data splits are not reported for either the zero-shot or the few-shot evaluation protocol; the K-shot support images may therefore share patients with the held-out test set, artificially inflating measured performance. Reported results further appear to reflect single runs, without seeds, confidence intervals, or standard deviations — a concern that is especially acute for few-shot sample selection, which is known to be highly variance-sensitive.
G11. Metrics are too narrow for clinical readiness: Only image-level and pixel-level AUC are reported. The paper does not report Dice, IoU, or PRO scores; thresholded accuracy, F1, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, or NPV; false positives per patient; calibration or expected calibration error (ECE); or prevalence-adjusted and rare-category performance. AUC alone can obscure poor performance under severe class imbalance and does not by itself demonstrate clinical utility.
G12. Baselines and benchmark details are incomplete: Missing comparisons include PatchCore under a few-shot normal-only setting, full CLIP fine-tuning, and other vision-language-model adaptation methods. In-domain MVTec is evaluated only under the few-shot regime, with zero-shot in-domain evaluation absent entirely. The benchmark is described only as “based on BMAD,” without specifying official splits, which limits comparability across future work.
G13. Scalability, memory, and privacy considerations are unaddressed: The method uses a CLIP ViT-L/14 backbone and trains six separate leave-one-out models for 50 epochs each on a single RTX 3090 GPU; training and inference time, memory footprint, and parameter counts are not reported. The term “lightweight” refers only to the adapters, not to the overall system. The few-shot memory bank grows with K and with spatial resolution, yet retrieval cost and the privacy and governance implications of storing patient-derived features are not analyzed. Downscaling to a 240 × 240 resolution and processing volumetric data as 2D slices may cause small lesions and broader 3D CT/MRI context to be lost.
G14. Cross-domain, acquisition, and modality generalism is limited: Evaluation covers brain MRI, liver CT, retinal OCT, chest X-ray, and histopathology; ultrasound, PET, mammography, and dermoscopy are not modeled, nor are shifts in acquisition device, site, or imaging protocol. The medical-specific, text-prompt-dependent design may generalize poorly to broader semantic or medical anomaly types and to combined industrial-and-medical generalist settings.
G15. Interpretability and clinical validation are absent: The model outputs anomaly scores and maps only, without language-based reasoning, radiological explanation, or multimodal-LLM-style justification. The paper provides no external or multi-institution validation, no prospective or reader study, no demographic (sex, age), scanner, or site fairness analysis, no uncertainty or failure-mode analysis, and no discussion of regulatory or clinical-workflow integration or independent clinical- precision assessment; prior evaluations in the literature suggest that CLIP-based zero-shot anomaly detection precision may fall short of clinical requirements.
